metadata.title: Education, Labour Market Experience and Cognitive Skills (EN)

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses OECD’s PIAAC microdata (adults 16–65) for multiple countries, with a pooled analytic sample restricted to prime-age respondents (26–45) and, in some specifications, to 16–45 or 16–65. The paper does not report the use of PIAAC sampling weights or any replicate-weight scheme (e.g., BRR/jackknife), so the weighting approach is not transparent from the provided text. For analysts working with PIAAC public-use data, the recommended practice is to apply the provided sampling weights to obtain population-representative estimates and to use replicate weights (if available in the dataset) for correct uncertainty under the complex survey design. Because the manuscript’s estimation strategy is regression-based with fixed effects and country dummies, weight omission (if it occurred) could affect standard errors and the generalizability of effect sizes across countries.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper states that it uses only one of the ten imputations of the PIAAC score for each test (preliminary results), but it does not describe a full plausible-values combining procedure (e.g., Rubin’s rules) or a specific missing-data handling method beyond that single-imputation choice. Because the dependent variables are numeracy and literacy test scores derived from PIAAC’s scoring/imputation framework, the manuscript does not provide enough detail to map the approach to a specific PV-handling category in the schema. This is therefore treated as a reporting gap for missing-data/PV-combination transparency.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Uses PIAAC adults 16–65, but the baseline descriptive statistics and many regressions restrict to prime-aged respondents 26–45. The paper pools employed and unemployed respondents and includes both literacy and numeracy domains (problem solving in technology-rich environments is not used because it is not administered in all countries). For some regressions, the sample is further restricted to 16–45 or expanded to 16–65, and the analysis focuses on schooling groups (basic/“bachelor”/college) and on task measures from the current or last job. Individuals who took the exam on paper are controlled with a dummy in regressions. The paper also notes that it uses only one of the ten imputations of the score for each test (preliminary results), but it does not specify additional missing-data exclusions beyond that.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD working paper uses PIAAC 2012 adult literacy and numeracy assessments (computer or paper administration) to study how formal education and labour-market experience relate to cognitive skills. The analysis focuses on eight countries with the largest samples (Spain, Italy, United Kingdom/England & Northern Ireland, Ireland, Norway, Sweden, Estonia, Netherlands), with additional regressions including several other countries. The baseline analytic sample is prime-aged adults (26–45), and some models use broader age ranges (16–45 or 16–65). The paper uses one of the ten imputations for each test score (preliminary results) and constructs work experience from years in paid work (≥6 months) and job task content from reported task frequency in the current/last job, distinguishing basic vs advanced numeracy and literacy tasks. Results indicate that experience is most strongly associated with numeracy early in the career for low-educated adults, and that performing basic numeracy/literacy tasks is linked to higher corresponding test performance mainly among the least schooled; overall, on-the-job learning is estimated to be about one-third of the contribution of compulsory schooling. The paper is regression/econometric rather than ML-predictive, and it does not report a full PV/missing-data combining strategy or survey-weight usage in the provided text, limiting strict comparability of effect sizes and uncertainty across countries.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This is an OECD report using econometric regression strategies (including fixed effects and country dummies) rather than machine-learning predictive modeling. The provided text does not describe any ML algorithm training/evaluation pipeline, and therefore main_findings are intentionally left empty to avoid fabricating ML-style performance metrics. The extraction is dense on assessment constructs and regression outcomes, but sparse on survey-weight application and on explicit PV/missing-data combination rules, which is why PV handling is treated as not_applicable and missing-data handling is not_reported.
